query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a small amount of silicon (~0.5–1 at.%) into a CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy will promote the in situ formation of a continuous, adaptive SiO2 glaze during sliding, thereby ensuring a low friction coefficient and reduced wear rate consistently from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional, homogeneous CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with no added reactive elements.
generation.intervention: Alloying the CoCrFeNi matrix with a trace level of silicon (approximately 0.5–1 at.%), integrated during synthesis.
generation.conditions: Dry sliding tests conducted in ambient air over a wide temperature range (room temperature to 800 °C) under varied loads and sliding speeds that generate moderate frictional heating.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of an ultrathin, amorphous SiO2 tribolayer at the sliding interface that self-replenishes under shear and protects against direct metal–metal contact.
generation.mechanism: Under sliding conditions, frictional heating and shear stress activate the oxidation of the trace Si in the matrix. The resulting SiO2 forms a lubricious and thermally stable glaze layer that lowers interfacial shear strength, thereby continuously mitigating wear and friction across a broad temperature window.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy, the Si-doped variant is predicted to exhibit a significantly reduced coefficient of friction (potentially on the order of 20–30% lower, though precise values are uncertain) and lower wear rates (possibly by an order of magnitude improvement) across the temperature range from RT to 800 °C.
generation.baseline: Standard friction and wear performance of the unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy tested under identical sliding, load, and temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective in dry, oxidizing environments where frictional heating facilitates Si oxidation; however, its benefit may be limited in inert atmospheres or under conditions where the heat is insufficient to trigger rapid oxidation.
generation.uncertainty: The hypothesis builds on the concept of reactive wear protection via in situ oxide formation (extended from evidence in PMC8448869::web::003 and PMC10241162::web::036) and extrapolates it to promote a lubricious SiO2 film in CoCrFeNi; uncertainties remain regarding the detailed oxidation kinetics of Si under dynamic sliding conditions and its influence on phase stability compared to other reactive additions (as contrasted in PMC6266227::web::004).

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of samples: one with the standard CoCrFeNi alloy (control) and one with 0.5–1 at.% Si addition. Subject both sets to ball-on-disk sliding tests under dry ambient conditions over a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C, while varying load and sliding speed. Characterize the worn surfaces via SEM and XPS to detect the formation and continuity of a SiO2 layer.
measurements: Time-resolved coefficient of friction data at various temperatures
Surface chemical analysis (XPS/EDS) to confirm the presence and uniformity of SiO2 on the wear track
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Si-doped CoCrFeNi samples do not show a statistically significant (e.g., >20% reduction) improvement in friction and wear metrics across the full temperature range relative to the control, or if surface analysis fails to identify a continuous, lubricious SiO2 layer, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Therefore, the cooperative heterostructure in the NiX activates the dense nanocrystalline glaze layer during high-temperature wear, thus minimizing the adhesive and oxidative wear between the tribo-pairs. From the above analyses, the underlying wear mechanisms responsible for the unprecedented wear resistance in the NiX are schematically illustrated in Fig. S23. During sliding at RT, the intrinsic structures of NiX rely on multiple deformation pathways to evoke the NC tribo-layer and the UFG tribo-layer, thus progressively accommodating the gradient elastic–plastic deformation distributed along the friction interface. During sliding at 800 °C, the intrinsic structures of NiX are able to promote the formation of a dense glaze layer and a deformed tribo-layer containing alumina nanoparticles and amorphous oxides through spontaneous tribochemical reactions, which dramatically suppress adhesive and oxidative wear between tribo-pairs.

Here, we propose an alloy design concept based on an enthalpy-guided approach to promote formation of solid solution nanocrystals, rather than crystalline oxide nanoparticles, in the amorphous matrix during wear. This structure enables a high strength and homogeneous plastic deformation of the friction-induced oxidic nanocomposite surface layer. We realize this concept in a multi-component (TiNbZr)75Ag25 (at.%) alloy, by blending a TiNbZr medium-entropy alloy with Ag to create the desired self-lubricating nanostructure upon wear exposure. A ball-on-disk sliding test at a maximum contact stress of 1.0 GPa reveals that the (TiNbZr)75Ag25 alloy exhibits a friction coefficient of around 0.09 in air. The tribological contact introduces environmental O into the alloy, facilitating new atomic coordination with large negative enthalpy of mixing, which enhances the alloy’s glass-forming ability. Besides, Ag has a positive enthalpy of mixing with Nb (+16 kJ/mol), which serves as a thermodynamic driving force for the nucleation of Ag nanocrystals from the amorphous matrix.
